title: Sorting Algorithms
tagline: Five classic sorting algorithms, their complexity trade-offs, and why choosing the right one still matters in production code.

sections.content:
Sorting is the gateway algorithm topic: deceptively simple to state (put items in order), rich enough to expose every major complexity trade-off. Every language runtime ships a highly-optimised sort, yet interviews and systems work still demand that you understand *why* merge sort beats bubble sort by a factor of a million on large inputs, and when a naïve insertion sort is actually the right call.

Five algorithms cover the conceptual landscape: **bubble sort** and **selection sort** (O(n²), educational), **insertion sort** (O(n²) worst, O(n) best — useful for nearly-sorted data), **merge sort** (O(n log n) guaranteed, stable, extra space), and **quicksort** (O(n log n) average, O(1) extra space, unstable, O(n²) worst case). JavaScript's `Array.prototype.sort` uses TimSort — a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort — giving O(n log n) worst-case with stability.

sections.title: Sorting a Hand of Playing Cards
sections.content:
Picture holding seven cards face-down. You flip them one by one and slot each card into its correct position among the cards already in your hand — that is **insertion sort**. It is natural, fast when the hand is nearly ordered, but slow when the deck is shuffled.

Now imagine splitting the deck in half, giving each half to a friend to sort independently, then merging the two sorted halves back together by comparing top cards — that is **merge sort**. The work is divided logarithmically (each split halves the problem), and the merge is linear, giving O(n log n) overall. **Quicksort** is like picking one card as a pivot, putting smaller cards to the left and larger to the right, then repeating for each side — fast on average, but unlucky pivot choice can degenerate to O(n²).

**Bubble sort** repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order elements until no swaps remain. Each pass "bubbles" the largest unsorted element to its final position. Time complexity is O(n²) in the average and worst case, O(n) in the best case (already sorted with an early-exit flag). It is stable (equal elements never swap) but has no production use — its only virtue is pedagogical simplicity.

**Selection sort** finds the minimum element in the unsorted portion and swaps it to the front, shrinking the unsorted portion by one each pass. Unlike bubble sort it makes exactly n−1 swaps, which is useful if writes are expensive (e.g., flash memory). It is O(n²) in all cases and *not* stable in the standard implementation. **Insertion sort** takes the next element and shifts larger elements right to create its slot — like inserting a card into a sorted hand. Best case O(n) (already sorted), worst O(n²) (reverse sorted). Stable, in-place, and extremely fast for small n or nearly-sorted data — which is why TimSort switches to it below a threshold.

**Merge sort** splits the array in half recursively until sub-arrays are length 1 (trivially sorted), then merges pairs of sorted sub-arrays bottom-up. Each merge level processes all n elements, and there are log₂ n levels, giving O(n log n) in all cases. Crucially it is **stable** — equal elements preserve their original relative order — making it the right choice for multi-key sorting. The downside is O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step. **Quicksort** picks a pivot, partitions elements (smaller left, larger right), then recurses on each partition. Average case O(n log n) with small constants and excellent cache behaviour (in-place partition). Worst case O(n²) when the pivot is always the minimum or maximum — mitigated by random pivot selection or median-of-three. Quicksort is not stable.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: mergeSort is non-destructive (returns a new array) because slice creates copies. The `<=` in merge is the stability guarantee — when elements are equal the left element (which appeared earlier) comes first. quickSort is in-place: it swaps elements within the original array. Random pivot selection makes worst-case O(n²) astronomically unlikely in practice.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Stability** is the property that equal elements preserve their original relative order after sorting. It matters whenever you sort by one key and then sort the result by another — a stable sort on the second key keeps the first-key order intact within ties. JavaScript's `Array.prototype.sort` has been guaranteed stable since ECMAScript 2019 (V8 uses TimSort). When in doubt, reach for `Array.sort` — it is O(n log n) worst-case and stable.

items: Bubble, selection, and insertion sort are O(n²) — fine for tiny inputs (n < 20), unusable at scale.
Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases and is stable, at the cost of O(n) auxiliary space.
Quicksort is O(n log n) average with excellent cache performance and O(1) extra space, but is not stable and degrades to O(n²) without random pivot selection.
A **stable** sort preserves the original order of equal elements — critical for multi-key sorting; JavaScript's built-in sort (TimSort) is stable since ES2019.
TimSort — used by JavaScript, Python, and Java — is a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort, achieving O(n) on nearly-sorted data and O(n log n) worst case.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort always splits the array into halves (log n levels) and merges them (O(n) per level), giving O(n log n) in best, average, and worst cases — unlike quicksort which can degrade to O(n²).

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm is NOT stable in its standard implementation?
quiz.explanation: Selection sort swaps the minimum element into position, which can disrupt the relative order of equal elements. Bubble sort, insertion sort, and merge sort are all stable when implemented with a strict '<=' comparison.

quiz.question: Why does quicksort use random pivot selection?
options: To reduce memory usage from O(n) to O(1)
To avoid the O(n²) worst case triggered by always picking the min or max pivot
To guarantee O(n log n) in all cases
quiz.explanation: When the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., on already-sorted input), one partition gets all n-1 remaining elements and the recursion is O(n) deep — O(n²) total. Random pivot makes this pathological case astronomically unlikely.

quiz.question: For which input does insertion sort outperform merge sort in practice?
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly-sorted data (few elements out of place = few shifts) and has a tiny constant factor that beats merge sort's overhead for small n. TimSort exploits this by switching to insertion sort below a threshold (~32–64 elements).

quiz.question: What extra space does merge sort require beyond the input array?
quiz.explanation: The merge step must create a temporary array to hold merged results — O(n) total across all active merge calls at any given recursion level. This is merge sort's main disadvantage compared to in-place algorithms like quicksort.

quiz.question: What is TimSort (used by JavaScript's Array.sort)?
options: A time-limited variant of bubble sort
A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort with O(n log n) worst-case
quiz.explanation: TimSort detects existing sorted runs in the input, extends short runs with insertion sort, then merges them using merge sort logic. It achieves O(n) on already-sorted data and O(n log n) worst-case, and is stable.

quiz.question: You must sort an array of 1 million records by last name, then by first name within the same last name. Which property of the sorting algorithm is essential?
quiz.explanation: Sort by first name first (stable sort), then sort by last name (stable sort). Stability guarantees that equal last names preserve the first-name order from step 1. An unstable sort would scramble first names within the same last name.

quiz.question: What is the best-case time complexity of bubble sort (with early-exit optimisation)?
quiz.explanation: With the early-exit flag: if a full pass completes with zero swaps, the array is already sorted and the algorithm terminates. On an already-sorted array, one pass of n-1 comparisons occurs with no swaps — O(n).

quiz.question: Which algorithm makes exactly n-1 swaps regardless of input, making it suitable when writes are expensive?
quiz.explanation: Selection sort always finds the minimum of the unsorted portion and swaps it once per pass — exactly n-1 swaps total. Bubble sort can make up to O(n²) swaps; insertion sort shifts rather than swaps; merge sort requires auxiliary storage writes.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of quicksort's call stack in the average case?
quiz.explanation: Each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack. With a balanced partition (average case), the recursion depth is O(log n), so the stack uses O(log n) space. In the worst case (all elements in one partition), depth is O(n).
